items.label: section_header
items.text: HOW TO BALANCE EQUATIONS

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: This is really important! You must never, never change a formula when balancing an equation. All you are allowed to do is to write big numbers in front of the formula.

items.label: section_header
items.text: Try again:

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 5.5 A balanced equation for the reaction between methane and oxygen.

items.label: text
items.text: There are now the same number of each type of atom before and after. This is called balancing the equation.

items.label: text
items.text: In symbols, this equation would be:

items.label: formula
items.text: C H _ { 4 } + 2 O _ { 2 } \rightarrow C O _ { 2 } + 2 H _ { 2 } O

items.label: text
items.text: Think of each symbol (C or H or O) as representing one atom of that element. Count them up in the equation, and check that there is the same number of atoms on both sides.

items.label: text
items.text: In order to balance equations you should adopt a systematic approach.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Work across the equation from left to right, checking one element after ano t  s         ln that case, leave the element until the end and you will often find that it has sorted itself out.

items.label: list_item
items.text: If you have a group of atoms (like a sulfate group (SO₄), for example), which is unchanged from one side of the equation to the other, there is no reason why you can't just count that up as a whole group, rather than counting individual sulfurs and oxygens. It saves time.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Check everything at the end to make sure you haven't changed something that you have already counted.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXAMPLE1

items.label: text
items.text: Balance the equation for the reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid:

items.label: formula
items.text: Z n + H C I \rightarrow Z n C I _ { 2 } + H _ { 2 }

items.label: text
items.text: Work from left to right. Count the zinc atoms: 1 on each side; no problem!

items.label: text
items.text: Count the hydrogen atoms: 1 on the left, 2 on the right. If you have 2 at the end, you must have started with 2. The only way of achieving this is to have 2HCl. (You must not change the formula to H2Cl because this substance does not exist.)

items.label: formula
items.text: Z n + 2 H C l \rightarrow Z n C l _ { 2 } + H _ { 2 }

items.label: text
items.text: Now count the chlorines: there are 2 on each side. Good! Finally check everything again to make sure and you've finished.
